presentingComplaint: Acute abdominal distension, vomiting and increasing confusion in a nursing-home resident with advanced dementia and permanent atrial fibrillation.
history: 81-year-old woman brought from her care home after 6 hours of vomiting, abdominal distension and an acute deterioration in her baseline confusion. She has advanced dementia (non-verbal, cannot localise or rate pain), permanent atrial fibrillation and prior heart failure. Long-term warfarin was stopped 3 months ago after a fall with a head injury, and she is currently on aspirin only. Carers noted she was clutching her abdomen and moaning, appeared distressed, and had two episodes of loose dark stool. The confounding comorbidities (advanced dementia obscuring the classic 'pain out of proportion' history, and AF managed off anticoagulation) delayed recognition; initial triage attributed the picture to constipation and a possible chest infection. There is no prior abdominal surgery and no reported fever.
examination: Frail, agitated and non-communicative. Irregularly irregular pulse. Abdomen is distended and tympanitic with sluggish bowel sounds; palpation elicits marked distress and guarding that appears disproportionate to the relatively soft, non-peritonitic abdominal wall on early examination. No pulsatile mass. Peripheries cool and mottled with delayed capillary refill. No focal neurological deficit beyond baseline dementia.
imaging: Erect chest and supine abdominal X-ray non-specific with mildly dilated small-bowel loops and no free air. CT angiography of the abdomen (arterial + portal-venous phases) shows an abrupt filling defect in the proximal superior mesenteric artery just beyond the origin with non-opacification of distal branches, several non-enhancing (poorly perfused) jejunal/ileal segments, and mesenteric fat stranding without pneumatosis or portal venous gas - findings of embolic superior mesenteric artery occlusion with early bowel ischemia.
microbiology: Blood cultures sent; no growth at time of assessment. This is a non-infective vascular emergency; leukocytosis reflects ischemia rather than primary infection.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute mesenteric ischemia (embolic SMA occlusion) - favoured: AF off anticoagulation, severe metabolic (lactic) acidosis and distress out of proportion to a soft abdomen, CT angiographic filling defect
Small-bowel obstruction - distension and dilated loops, but does not explain profound lactic acidosis or the arterial filling defect
Acute pancreatitis - amylase normal, no CT features
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm - no pulsatile mass, aorta normal calibre on CT
Sepsis of intra-abdominal source - considered given leukocytosis and shock physiology, but arterial occlusion is the primary lesion
finalDiagnosis: Acute mesenteric ischemia due to embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery (cardioembolic, from atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation), presenting atypically because advanced dementia masked the classic pain history.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency (Acute Intestinal Ischemia)
World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) - Acute Mesenteric Ischemia Guidelines - 2017
European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) - Management of the Diseases of Mesenteric Arteries and Veins - 2017
stewardship: Non-infective vascular emergency; empiric antibiotics are not the definitive therapy. Management is immediate resuscitation, systemic anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin, and urgent revascularisation (endovascular or surgical embolectomy) with assessment of bowel viability. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are given only as peri-operative adjunct for anticipated bacterial translocation/resection, not as the primary treatment - so no stewardship tier is assigned to this diagnostic case.
contraindications: Avoid delaying CT angiography for stool softeners/enema on an assumption of constipation
Avoid vasopressors that worsen splanchnic vasoconstriction (e.g. high-dose norepinephrine/vasopressin) where volume resuscitation is adequate
Do not withhold anticoagulation on the basis of the remote prior head injury once active haemorrhage is excluded
Avoid nephrotoxic contrast overload without renal-protective measures given AKI, but do not omit essential CT angiography
edgeCases: Advanced dementia removes the hallmark 'pain out of proportion' history, so lactate and clinical distress must drive suspicion
Normal or minimally elevated amylase/lactate early can falsely reassure; lactate rises only once transmural infarction begins
Absence of pneumatosis or portal venous gas does not exclude early ischemia - these are late signs
Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI) is the alternative mechanism in low-flow states; here the discrete SMA filling defect confirms an embolic occlusive cause
expectedMaiK: Recognise a vascular abdominal catastrophe (acute mesenteric ischemia) from the triad of atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation, severe lactic acidosis, and abdominal distress disproportionate to exam findings; obtain urgent CT angiography and involve vascular surgery immediately rather than treating as constipation/obstruction.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the patient anticoagulated, and what is the AF/embolic history?
What is the serum lactate and arterial blood gas (degree of metabolic acidosis)?
Is there abdominal distension, guarding, or distress out of proportion to palpation?
Any per-rectal blood or dark stool, and prior abdominal surgery?
Time of symptom onset (to gauge bowel-salvage window)?
expectedInvestigations: CT angiography of the abdomen (arterial + portal-venous phases)
Serum lactate and arterial blood gas
Full blood count, urea/electrolytes, creatinine, amylase/lipase
